scores.text: What is an intent to file?
scores.reply: An intent to file is a notice to VA that you plan to file a claim for disability compensation, pension, or Dependency and Indemnity Compensation. It sets a potential start date for any benefits you may later receive. If you file your complete claim within one year, VA can use the date it received your intent to file as that start date, which may allow back payments if the claim is approved. You can submit one online, by phone, in person, or by mail on VA Form 21-0966. This comes from VA's page at va.gov/resources/your-intent-to-file-a-va-claim/. Your file shows that we filed an intent to file for you on October 12, 2026, and it holds until October 12, 2027.

scores.text: How long does a higher-level review take?
scores.reply: VA's stated goal is to finish Higher-Level Reviews that aren't about healthcare benefits in an average of about 125 days, or roughly 4 to 5 months. How long it takes can vary depending on the type of benefit decision and whether an informal conference is requested, which can add time. This is VA's average goal, not a promise for your review. The source is VA's website pages on Higher-Level Review (va.gov/decision-reviews/higher-level-review) and choosing a decision review option (va.gov/resources/choosing-a-decision-review-option). Your attorney can talk through which review option fits your situation.

scores.text: What is a C-file?
scores.reply: A C-file, also called a claims file, is the folder VA keeps for a veteran's claim. It holds the evidence and documents tied to that claim. According to VA's FOIA guidance, veterans can request their C-file to see what VA has on record for their claim. Your case snapshot shows that our team has already read your claims file. If you have questions about what is in it, tell me and I can pass that along to a person on our team.

scores.text: Can I revoke the 21-22a later if I want?
scores.reply:
Yes. According to VA's accredited representative FAQ (va.gov) and 38 CFR 14.631 (eCFR), a power of attorney can be revoked at any time, and an attorney or agent can be discharged at any time.

VA says you can cancel by:
- Calling 800-827-1000
- Mailing a letter to the Claims Intake Center in Janesville, WI
- Faxing a letter

VA suggests telling the former representative right away as well.

I can't cancel or change anything on your case myself. This is general information, not legal advice. If you're thinking about revoking, a person on our team can talk through what that would mean for your claim. Just let me know and I'll pass that along.

scores.text: Do you charge anything up front?
scores.reply:
Generally, no. VA-accredited attorneys cannot charge fees for an initial claim. Under VA's rules, fees can only be charged after VA has decided the claim, a fee agreement is signed, and a VA Form 21-22a naming the attorney is on file (source: va.gov, VA-accredited representative FAQs). VA also warns that anyone who asks for an upfront payment to help with a VA claim is likely running a scam.

Our fee is contingent: 30% of past-due benefits, paid directly by you to the firm. The fee agreement you signed on October 10 has the full terms. If you have questions about it, a person on our team can go over it with you.

scores.text: Should I go to my C&P exam?
scores.reply:
Here is general information from VA's website and the federal regulation on C&P exams (sources: va.gov/resources/va-claim-exam/ and 38 CFR 3.655). A C&P exam is a medical exam VA may ask for to learn more about a claimed condition. Not every claim needs one. If a veteran misses a scheduled exam, the claim can be delayed, and VA may decide it based on the evidence already in the file. There are exceptions for good cause, such as hospitalization, terminal illness, homelessness, or the death of an immediate family member.

I can't advise you on whether to go to your exam, and I can't see any exam scheduling in your file. A person on our team will follow up with you about any exam tied to your claim.

scores.text: What is a supplemental claim?
scores.reply:
A supplemental claim is a way to ask VA to review a decision you disagree with. You can do this by submitting new and relevant evidence, meaning information VA has not considered before that could change the outcome. You can also use it to ask VA to review your claim based on a change in law, such as the PACT Act. This comes from the VA page on supplemental claims at va.gov (https://www.va.gov/decision-reviews/supplemental-claim/).

I can't advise whether a supplemental claim makes sense for your situation. A person on our team is already handling your case, so if you want to talk through whether it fits, they can follow up with you on that.

scores.text: What is my effective date?
scores.reply:
I can't give you your specific effective date, because it depends on facts in your claim that our team is still reviewing, and I don't want to guess at it.

Here is the general rule from VA's website. For a direct service connection claim, the effective date is generally the later of two dates: the date VA receives your claim, or the date your illness or injury first began. If your claim is received within one year of leaving service, the effective date can go back to the day after you separated (source: va.gov/disability/effective-date/).

Your intent to file, which we submitted on 2026-10-12, sets a potential start date for your benefits. You then have until 2027-10-12 to submit your completed claim (source: va.gov/resources/your-intent-to-file-a-va-claim/).

scores.text: Can I add my wife as a dependent?

A spouse can be added in one of two ways: by filing a dependency claim online through eBenefits with a Premium account, or by mailing VA Form 21-686c, the Application Request to Add and/or Remove Dependents. You will need your marriage date and location as shown on the marriage certificate. If the marriage was common law, tribal, or by proxy, VA asks for additional documents with the claim.

Sources: va.gov (disability/add-remove-dependent and manage-dependents pages) and VA Form 21-686c.

- To add a spouse, you can file online through eBenefits, or by submitting VA Form 21-674.
